title: Conduct treatment processes for weeds and invader plants

lessons.title: Preparing the clearing team and site
lessons.html:
Starting with the plan

Weed and invader plant treatment in practice may mean spraying weeds on a silo hardstand, clearing wattle from a riverbank on a farm, treating prickly pear in the Karoo veld or controlling regrowth along fence lines. Begin with the approved plan: map of areas, target species, methods, registered herbicides, rates, team size, schedule and follow-up.

Site checks

  • Walk the site with the landowner. Confirm boundaries and target species, and identify indigenous plants to protect.
  • Mark watercourses, wetlands, boreholes, crops, gardens and beehives, with buffer zones.
  • Identify hazards: steep slopes, rocks, snakes, bees, dense thickets, power lines, livestock and wildlife.
  • Locate the mixing area away from water on level ground, and the vehicle parking and first aid points.
  • Check weather: wind, rain and temperature suitable for the herbicide and method.

Team preparation

Brief the team on species identification using samples or photos so they do not damage indigenous plants. Assign tasks such as felling, stacking, herbicide application and supervision. Check PPE: chemical gloves, overalls, boots and eye protection for herbicide applicators; chainsaw chaps, helmet with visor and ear protection, and gloves for saw operators. Only trained and authorised workers may operate chainsaws and brushcutters.

Preparing herbicide

  1. Read the label: registered species, technique, rate, adjuvant, PPE and restrictions near water.
  2. Calibrate knapsacks with water before the day's work.
  3. Mix the calculated quantity, adding dye where permitted so treated plants and stumps are visible.
  4. Label every knapsack and container with its contents.

lessons.title: Applying treatment methods
lessons.html:
Matching method to plant size and type

PlantTypical method
Seedlings and small plantsHand pull (with roots) or foliar spray
Saplings and shrubsFoliar spray or basal stem treatment
TreesFell and cut stump treatment, or frill or stem injection for standing trees
Dense regrowthFoliar spray of actively growing coppice
Succulents such as prickly pearMethods and products registered for the species; biocontrol where established

Cut stump treatment

  1. Fell the tree safely, with a planned felling direction and escape route, keeping other workers at least two tree lengths away.
  2. Cut the stump low and level.
  3. Apply herbicide to the freshly cut surface immediately, as the label requires, because delays reduce uptake. For many species the cambium ring just inside the bark is the critical area.
  4. Dyed herbicide shows which stumps have been treated.

Foliar spraying

  • Spray to wet the leaves evenly but not to run-off.
  • Keep the nozzle low and use coarse droplets to limit drift.
  • Do not spray stressed, dusty or wet plants if the label warns against it.
  • Avoid spraying indigenous plants and keep out of buffer zones.

Basal stem and frill treatments

Apply basal stem treatments to the lower stem bark all round the stem at the height the label states. For frill treatment, make downward cuts through the bark around the stem and apply herbicide into the cuts immediately.

Handling cut material

Stack cut material away from watercourses and roads. Remove seed-bearing branches where possible to avoid spreading seed. Do not burn without permission and fire precautions.

lessons.title: Completing the job and follow-up
lessons.html:
End of day

  • Count tools and equipment and check them for damage.
  • Clean knapsacks at the mixing area, spraying rinse water onto treated areas as allowed, never into water.
  • Secure empty containers for correct disposal.
  • Wash hands and face, and change and wash work clothes.
  • Check for injuries, bites or chemical exposure and record them.

Records

Record the areas treated on the map, species, density, methods, herbicide and registration number, quantity used, number of person-days, weather and observations. Take photographs at fixed points before and after treatment.

Follow-up treatment

Return when the label indicates full effect should be visible to assess kill rate and treat survivors. Schedule follow-ups for seedlings from the seed bank and coppice regrowth, often several times over several years. Initial clearing without follow-up is usually wasted effort.

Rehabilitation

Recommend steps to restore cover: allow indigenous vegetation to recover, re-seed with suitable grasses, and manage grazing and fire so that cleared areas do not reinvade. On slopes and riverbanks, protect the soil against erosion.

Key points

  • Confirm target species, buffer zones and hazards with the landowner before starting.
  • Only trained workers use chainsaws and brushcutters, with full protective gear.
  • Apply cut stump treatment immediately after felling and use dye to mark treated stumps.
  • Spray to wet without run-off, using coarse droplets and avoiding indigenous plants.
  • Record treatments, follow up regularly and rehabilitate cleared land.

quiz.question: Why is dye added to herbicide where permitted?

options.text: To show which plants and stumps have been treated

quiz.question: When should herbicide be applied to a cut stump?

options.text: After the stump dries out completely

quiz.question: How far should other workers keep from a tree being felled?

options.text: Close enough to help catch it

quiz.question: How should foliar spray be applied?

options.text: Until the herbicide drips to the ground
As a fine mist from high above
To wet the leaves evenly but not to run-off
At the mixing area, with rinse water sprayed onto treated areas

quiz.question: Follow-up treatments over several years are usually needed after initial clearing.
